report:
**Conclusion: No.** Reliable evidence does not show that ivermectin lowers the risk of death from COVID-19.

Why the belief arose: some early, generally small studies and observational analyses reported fewer deaths. But such studies are especially vulnerable to bias (for example, differences in patient severity, other treatments, and reporting), and some influential early ivermectin research later faced serious reliability concerns. A mortality claim requires well-randomized, adequately sized trials and systematic reviews that prioritize them.

The larger, placebo-controlled TOGETHER randomized trial tested early ivermectin in higher-risk outpatients and was designed to detect clinically important progression (hospital admission or prolonged emergency observation). It did **not** find a meaningful benefit. It therefore does not support a reduction in severe outcomes or death:  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2115869

Cochrane’s systematic review—an independent evidence synthesis—found the evidence for prevention and treatment conflicting, rather than establishing a mortality benefit:  
https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD015017.pub3/abstract

Consistent with this assessment, the Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends **against ivermectin** for both hospitalized and ambulatory COVID-19 patients outside a clinical trial, citing very-low-certainty evidence:  
https://www.idsociety.org/globalassets/idsa/practice-guidelines/covid-19/treatment/idsa-covid-19-gl-tx-and-mgmt---ivermectin-2022-10-10.pdf

This does not mean ivermectin is never useful: it is an effective prescription medicine for certain parasitic infections. But it is not an established COVID-19 treatment, and using animal formulations or inappropriate doses can cause harm. For someone at elevated risk with COVID-19, prompt discussion with a clinician about proven antivirals is the safer course.
